experiments.title: Digit span
experiments.hook: How many digits can you hold? Forwards, then backwards.
experiments.question: How much can short-term memory hold, and what changes when you have to work with it?
steps: Watch the digits appear one at a time.
Type them back. Two tries at each length.
Then do it again, but backwards.
experiments.finding: Most adults repeat about 6 or 7 digits forwards. Backwards is usually one or two fewer, because you have to hold the digits and rearrange them at the same time.
theory: Forward span mostly measures how much you can hold for a few seconds. Backward span adds work: you hold the list and reorder it. That extra work is what people mean by working memory.

The famous "seven, plus or minus two" was an early estimate. Later work suggests the true limit is nearer four chunks, and that we reach seven by grouping digits (like a phone number) and by rehearsing them under our breath.
clinic: Digit span is part of the attention and concentration check in the mental status examination, and a subtest of standard intelligence batteries.

A low span says attention is poor right now. It does not say why: delirium, anxiety, low mood, poor sleep, low effort or a language barrier can all lower it. Always read it alongside the rest of the MSE.
In delirium, attention is the core problem, so span often falls sharply and changes across the day.

evidence.note: Typical adult ranges are well replicated. The exact capacity limit (about 4 chunks vs 7 items) is still discussed.

refs: Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two. Psychological Review, 63(2), 81 to 97.
Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87 to 114.

checks.q: A patient repeats 7 digits forwards but only 3 backwards. What is the most useful first thought?
options: Holding is fine; working with the information is harder
checks.why: Forward span looks fine. Backward span adds manipulation, so the gap points at working memory and attention control. Check the rest of the MSE before concluding anything.

checks.q: Why can people often beat "seven" with practice?
checks.why: Chunking packs several digits into one unit, so the same small store holds more.

checks.q: A drowsy patient on day 2 after surgery has a span of 3 in the morning and 6 in the afternoon. What does this suggest?
checks.why: Attention that swings across the day is a hallmark of delirium, which is a medical emergency until proven otherwise.

experiments.reflect: Did you use a strategy (grouping, saying them aloud, picturing them)? How would anxiety in a real assessment change your score?

experiments.title: Serial position
experiments.hook: Learn a list, recall it. Which words survive?
experiments.question: Does a word's place in a list change how likely you are to remember it?
steps: Read 12 words, shown one at a time.
Type every word you remember, in any order.
Do three lists. Your curve builds as you go.
experiments.finding: Words at the start (primacy) and the end (recency) are remembered best, giving a U-shaped curve. If you wait and do something else before recalling, the end advantage shrinks, but the start advantage stays.
theory: Early words get more rehearsal, so they are more likely to make it into long-term memory. That is the primacy effect.
The last few words are still in short-term memory when recall starts, so they come out first and easily. That is the recency effect.

Because a delay wipes out recency but not primacy, the curve was early evidence that short-term and long-term memory behave differently. This two-store reading is useful but simplified: recency also appears in some long-term tasks.
clinic: Word-list recall tests are used in memory assessment. Looking at which words are recalled, not just how many, tells you more.
In practice: patients remember the start and end of a consultation best. Say the most important instruction first, and repeat it at the end.

evidence.note: The U-shaped curve is very robust. Whether it proves two separate memory stores is debated.

refs: Murdock, B. B. (1962). The serial position effect of free recall. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 64(5), 482 to 488.
Glanzer, M., & Cunitz, A. R. (1966). Two storage mechanisms in free recall. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 5(4), 351 to 360.

checks.q: A 30-second distraction task is added before recall. Which part of the curve drops?
checks.why: The end advantage relies on words still being in short-term memory. A distraction displaces them.

checks.q: Why are early words remembered well?
options: They are still in short-term memory
checks.why: Early words get rehearsed more often, which helps them enter long-term memory.

checks.q: You have 10 minutes to explain a new medicine to a family. Where do you put the one thing they must remember?
options: At the start, and again at the end
checks.why: Use both primacy and recency: open with it and close with it.

experiments.reflect: Look at your own curve. Did it look like the classic U? If not, what did you do differently (grouping, a story, recalling the last words first)?

experiments.title: Stroop
experiments.hook: Name the ink colour, not the word. Harder than it sounds.
experiments.question: What happens when a habit (reading) fights the task (naming the colour)?
steps: A colour word appears in coloured ink.
Press the button for the INK colour, as fast as you can.
About 40 rounds. Your speed is measured.
experiments.finding: People are slower, and make more mistakes, when the word and the ink disagree (the word RED in blue ink). The gap is usually around a tenth of a second or more.
theory: Reading is so practised that it happens automatically. To name the ink you have to hold back the word that pops into mind.
That holding back is called inhibition, one of the brain's control (executive) functions. The extra time you need on mismatched trials is the cost of that control.
clinic: Stroop-type tasks are used in neuropsychological assessment of executive function and attention.

An "emotional Stroop" uses emotional words (for example threat words) instead of colour words. Slower naming for those words has been used to study attention bias in anxiety. Treat individual results with caution: the task is good for group research but unreliable for judging one person.

evidence.note: The colour-word Stroop effect is one of the most replicated findings in psychology. The emotional Stroop is less reliable at the individual level.

refs: Stroop, J. R. (1935). Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 18(6), 643 to 662.
MacLeod, C. M. (1991). Half a century of research on the Stroop effect: An integrative review. Psychological Bulletin, 109(2), 163 to 203.

checks.q: Why are mismatched trials slower?
options: The colours are harder to see
Reading happens automatically and must be held back
checks.why: The automatic reading response competes with the colour-naming response; inhibiting it takes time.

checks.q: A child who is just learning to read shows a very small Stroop effect. Why?
checks.why: The effect depends on reading being automatic. Without that habit there is little to inhibit.

checks.q: Which function does the Stroop mainly tap?
checks.why: It is a classic test of inhibitory control.

experiments.reflect: Where in daily life do you have to override an automatic habit? What makes it easier or harder?

experiments.title: Spot the change
experiments.hook: A flash of coloured squares. Did one change? Measure your visual memory.
experiments.question: How many objects can you hold in visual memory at once?
steps: Coloured squares flash for half a second.
After a short blank they come back. Same, or did one change colour?
Displays have 2 to 8 squares, in mixed order.
experiments.finding: Accuracy is near perfect for small displays and falls once there are more than about three or four squares. A simple formula (K) turns your answers into an estimate of how many squares you held, usually about 3 to 4.
theory: Visual working memory seems to hold a small number of objects. Past that, you are partly guessing.
K corrects for guessing: it uses both hits (saying "changed" when it did) and false alarms (saying "changed" when it did not). That is why saying "changed" every time does not give a high score.
clinic: The idea of hits and false alarms is the same one behind sensitivity and specificity in screening tests. A clinician who calls every patient "depressed" catches every case but is useless.
Working-memory limits matter in teaching and in therapy: give one or two new ideas at a time, then check they landed.

evidence.note: The 3 to 4 item estimate is well replicated. Whether memory holds a fixed number of slots or a flexible pool of resource is actively debated.

refs: Luck, S. J., & Vogel, E. K. (1997). The capacity of visual working memory for features and conjunctions. Nature, 390, 279 to 281.
Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87 to 114.

checks.q: Someone says "changed" on every trial. Their hit rate is 100%. What is their K?
checks.why: Their false-alarm rate is also 100%, so hit minus false alarm is zero. K catches pure guessing.

checks.q: Which clinical idea is closest to hits and false alarms?
checks.why: Hits map to sensitivity; avoiding false alarms maps to specificity.

checks.q: Accuracy is 98% with 2 squares and 65% with 8. What explains the drop?
options: Capacity is exceeded, so later items are guessed
checks.why: Beyond about 3 to 4 objects, not everything can be held, so performance falls toward guessing.

experiments.reflect: Did you try to name the colours in your head? Would saying them aloud help or hurt, and why?

experiments.title: Müller-Lyer illusion
experiments.hook: Two equal lines. Make them look equal. Measure how far your eyes are fooled.
experiments.question: Does what we see match what is there, and does experience shape it?
steps: One line has fins. The other is plain.
Drag the slider until the plain line looks the same length.
Six rounds, fins in and fins out.
experiments.finding: With fins pointing out, the line looks longer, so people stretch the plain line too far. With fins pointing in, it looks shorter. The error is often 10 to 20 percent, and knowing about the illusion does not make it go away.
theory: Perception is not a camera. The brain uses cues (like corners and depth) to guess what is out there, and those guesses can mislead.
One explanation: the fins look like the corners of a room or building, so the brain reads one line as further away and scales it up. This explanation is popular but not settled.
Cross-cultural studies found smaller illusions in people from less "carpentered" (fewer straight-walled buildings) environments. These findings are debated; later work points to other factors too.
clinic: The illusion persists even when you know it is an illusion. That is a useful picture for explaining to a patient why knowing a fear is irrational does not switch it off.
It also shows why observation needs checking: what we perceive in a session is shaped by expectation.

evidence.note: The illusion itself is robust. Its cause, and the cultural differences, are debated.

refs: Müller-Lyer, F. C. (1889). Optische Urteilstäuschungen. Archiv für Physiologie, Supplement, 263 to 270.
Segall, M. H., Campbell, D. T., & Herskovits, M. J. (1966). The influence of culture on visual perception. Bobbs-Merrill.

checks.q: After learning the lines are equal, the illusion…
checks.why: Knowledge does not override early perceptual processing. That is what makes it a good teaching example.

checks.q: How strong is the evidence for the "carpentered world" explanation?
checks.why: It was influential and has some support, but other explanations compete. Present it as debated.

checks.q: What is the main lesson for clinical observation?
options: Perception is shaped by expectation, so check it
checks.why: We see partly what we expect. Write down what was observed, not what was inferred.

experiments.reflect: Think of a time you were sure you saw or heard something that turned out to be different. What filled the gap?

experiments.title: Reward schedules
experiments.hook: Pick a reward rule, watch the behaviour it builds. Then stop rewarding.
experiments.question: How does the timing of rewards shape how often, and how stubbornly, a behaviour happens?
steps: Choose a reward rule and run the simulation.
Watch the response line and the reward ticks.
Then switch rewards off and see which habit lasts.
experiments.finding: Variable schedules (rewards after an unpredictable number of responses) produce fast, steady responding that is slow to stop when rewards end. Fixed-interval schedules produce a pause after each reward and a speed-up before the next.
theory: In operant conditioning, behaviour that is followed by a reward becomes more likely. The rule that decides when rewards come is the schedule.
Ratio schedules reward the number of responses; interval schedules reward the first response after some time. Fixed means predictable; variable means unpredictable.
Behaviour that was rewarded only some of the time takes longer to fade when rewards stop. This is the partial reinforcement extinction effect.
This simulation is a teaching model drawn to show the classic shapes. It is not data from a real learner.
clinic: Gambling machines pay out on variable schedules, which helps explain why gambling is so hard to stop.
Contingency management (giving rewards for verified abstinence) is an evidence-based treatment in substance use. It works best with immediate, reliable rewards at first.

Parent training: if a child's tantrums are sometimes rewarded by giving in, they are on a variable schedule, and will be stubborn when the parent stops. Expect a short burst before they fade (the extinction burst).

evidence.note: Schedule effects are among the most replicated findings in learning. Clinical applications vary in strength; contingency management has strong evidence in substance use.

refs: Ferster, C. B., & Skinner, B. F. (1957). Schedules of reinforcement. Appleton-Century-Crofts.
Skinner, B. F. (1938). The behavior of organisms. Appleton-Century.

checks.q: Which schedule makes behaviour most resistant to stopping?
checks.why: Unpredictable rewards make it hard to tell that rewards have stopped, so responding continues.

checks.q: A parent stops giving in to tantrums. The tantrums get worse for two days. What is this?
checks.why: A short increase is expected when a reward stops. Warn parents in advance so they hold steady.

checks.q: A monthly salary is closest to which schedule?
checks.why: Payment comes after a fixed time, though the real-world fit is loose (you still have to work).

experiments.reflect: Pick one habit of your own (checking your phone, snacking). What schedule keeps it going?

experiments.title: Bias spotter
experiments.hook: Short clinical moments. Name the thinking trap, then the fix.
experiments.question: Which mental shortcuts lead clinicians astray, and what protects against them?
steps: Read a short clinical moment.
Name the thinking trap.
Choose the habit that would have prevented it.
experiments.finding: Fast, intuitive judgement is usually good enough, but it fails in predictable ways. Naming the trap, and having a habit that forces a second look, reduces some of these errors.
theory: Heuristics are mental shortcuts. They save effort and are often right, but they produce systematic errors called biases.

Anchoring: sticking to the first piece of information. Availability: judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind. Representativeness: judging by how much something looks like a typical case. Confirmation bias: looking for evidence that fits what you already think.
In clinical work two more matter: premature closure (stopping thinking once a diagnosis is reached) and diagnostic overshadowing (putting new symptoms down to a known mental illness or disability).
clinic: These errors can be serious: a physical illness missed in someone with a psychiatric label, or a risk missed because the first impression was reassuring.
Useful habits: ask "what else could this be?", keep a short differential, re-check vital physical causes, and review the case with someone who has not met the patient.
Evidence that de-biasing training reliably reduces errors is mixed. Checklists and structured reviews have more support than simply knowing about biases.

evidence.note: The heuristics are well described. How much training reduces clinical error is still being studied.

refs: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124 to 1131.
Croskerry, P. (2003). The importance of cognitive errors in diagnosis and strategies to minimize them. Academic Medicine, 78(8), 775 to 780.
Reiss, S., Levitan, G. W., & Szyszko, J. (1982). Emotional disturbance and mental retardation: Diagnostic overshadowing. American Journal of Mental Deficiency, 86(6), 567 to 574.

checks.q: Which habit has the best support for reducing diagnostic error?
checks.why: Awareness alone has weak evidence; structures that force a second look do better.

checks.q: A man with schizophrenia complains of new headaches. Staff say it is "part of his illness". What is the risk?
checks.why: New physical symptoms are being put down to the known mental illness without being checked.

checks.q: Heuristics are…
options: Shortcuts that are often right but fail predictably
checks.why: They are efficient and usually work, which is why their failures are easy to miss.

experiments.reflect: Which trap do you think you are most prone to? What one habit will you use in your next case?

experiments.title: Pavlov's bell
experiments.hook: Ring a bell before food. Watch a new response being learned, then fade, then come back.
experiments.question: How does a neutral sound come to trigger a response, and does that learning ever really go away?
steps: Pair the bell with food and watch the response grow.
Ring the bell alone until the response fades.
Let a day pass, then ring it again.
experiments.finding: The response grows quickly at first, then levels off (acquisition). With the bell alone it fades (extinction). After a rest it partly returns (spontaneous recovery), which shows extinction did not erase the first learning.
theory: Food (the unconditioned stimulus) causes salivation without any learning. The bell (the conditioned stimulus) starts out neutral. After pairings, the bell alone causes salivation: the conditioned response.

The Rescorla-Wagner model says learning is driven by surprise. Each trial changes the bell's strength by a fraction of the gap between what happened and what was expected. Big gap early, big change; small gap later, small change. That is why the curve bends and levels off.

Extinction is new learning ("the bell no longer means food") laid over the old learning, not the old learning being deleted. The new learning is weaker and more tied to time and place, so it partly fades after a rest. Relearning is also faster the second time.
A similar but different tone gets part of the response (generalisation). The more different the tone, the smaller the response.
This simulation is a teaching model with fixed settings. It is not data from a real animal.
clinic: Phobias can be learned this way: something neutral is paired with fear. In the classic "Little Albert" study, a baby was taught to fear a white rat. The study is now a lesson in ethics: there was no proper consent, the fear was never removed, and it would not be allowed today.

Exposure therapy is planned extinction: meeting the feared cue, safely and repeatedly, without the bad outcome. Because extinction is new learning, fear can return after a gap or in a new place. Varying the settings and planning for relapse helps.

Some people on chemotherapy develop a dislike of foods eaten before treatment, or feel sick on arriving at the hospital. This is learned taste aversion and conditioned nausea. Giving an unusual "scapegoat" food before treatment has been used to protect usual foods.

evidence.note: Acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery and generalisation are among the most replicated findings in psychology. The Rescorla-Wagner model explains many results but not all (for example, some effects of pre-exposure to the tone).

refs: Pavlov, I. P. (1927). Conditioned reflexes (G. V. Anrep, Trans.). Oxford University Press.

Rescorla, R. A., & Wagner, A. R. (1972). A theory of Pavlovian conditioning: Variations in the effectiveness of reinforcement and nonreinforcement. In A. H. Black & W. F. Prokasy (Eds.), Classical conditioning II: Current research and theory (pp. 64 to 99). Appleton-Century-Crofts.
Bouton, M. E. (2004). Context and behavioral processes in extinction. Learning & Memory, 11(5), 485 to 494.
Watson, J. B., & Rayner, R. (1920). Conditioned emotional reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 3(1), 1 to 14.
Garcia, J., & Koelling, R. A. (1966). Relation of cue to consequence in avoidance learning. Psychonomic Science, 4(3), 123 to 124.
Bernstein, I. L. (1978). Learned taste aversions in children receiving chemotherapy. Science, 200(4347), 1302 to 1303.

checks.q: After extinction, the bell is rung again the next day and the dog salivates a little. What is this?
checks.why: The response partly returns after a rest because extinction was new learning on top of the old, not erasure.

checks.q: In the Rescorla-Wagner model, why do early pairings change the response the most?
checks.why: Learning is proportional to the gap between what happens and what was expected. Early on, the gap is largest.

checks.q: A client finished exposure therapy for a dog phobia. Six months later, in a new city, the fear returns. What is the most useful reading?
options: Expected relapse: extinction is tied to time and place; plan a booster
checks.why: Fear can return after time or in a new setting. Varied practice and booster sessions are part of good exposure work.

experiments.reflect: Think of one cue (a smell, a song, a place) that triggers a feeling in you. Can you trace the pairing that taught it? Has it ever faded and come back?

experiments.title: Design the study
experiments.hook: A claim lands on your desk. Build a study that could really test it.
experiments.question: What does a study need before we can believe that a treatment caused the change?
steps: Read the claim.
Make six design choices. The meter shows how many threats you have closed.
Lock your design, then improve it if you can.
experiments.finding: Most weak claims come from studies without a fair comparison group. Random assignment, a believable control, a good measure taken before and after, and enough people close the biggest gaps. Even then, no single study is final.
theory: To say an app reduced anxiety, you need to rule out other reasons anxiety might drop. Each of those other reasons is a threat to validity.

Internal validity asks: did the treatment cause the change in this study? Comparison groups, random assignment and blinding protect it. External validity asks: does the result apply to other people and places? Who you sample protects it.
Random assignment is powerful because it balances the groups on average, even on things you never thought to measure.
Real trials add more: registering the plan in advance, ethics approval, informed consent, and reporting every outcome measured, not just the ones that worked.
clinic: Every new therapy, app or supplement you hear about makes a causal claim. Ask: compared with what, and who chose who got it?

Patients often come to treatment when they feel worst. They tend to improve somewhat anyway (regression to the mean, and natural recovery). This is why uncontrolled before-and-after results in clinics look better than trials.
In psychotherapy research, participants cannot be fully blind to what they receive. Good trials use an active comparison and keep the outcome rater blind instead.

evidence.note: These principles of research design are standard. The scores in this activity are a simplified teaching scheme; real judgement weighs threats differently in different studies.

refs: Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for generalized causal inference. Houghton Mifflin.
Orne, M. T. (1962). On the social psychology of the psychological experiment: With particular reference to demand characteristics and their implications. American Psychologist, 17(11), 776 to 783.
Barnett, A. G., van der Pols, J. C., & Dobson, A. J. (2005). Regression to the mean: What it is and how to deal with it. International Journal of Epidemiology, 34(1), 215 to 220.

checks.q: Students with the highest anxiety this week join a programme. Next month they score lower. What else could explain the drop?
checks.why: Extreme scores tend to move back towards average on re-testing, with or without treatment.

checks.q: Why is random assignment better than letting people choose their group?
options: It balances the groups on average, even on things not measured
checks.why: Choosers differ in motivation and more. Randomising spreads those differences evenly between groups.

checks.q: A trial compares a therapy with a waiting list. What does it NOT rule out?
checks.why: A waiting list controls for time passing, but not for the boost of getting attention and hope. An active comparison does.

experiments.reflect: Think of a health claim you saw recently (a reel, an advert, a forward). Which of the eight threats would you ask about first?

experiments.title: Correlation or cause?
experiments.hook: Six headlines, six scatter plots. Guess the link, then judge the claim.
experiments.question: When two things go together, when can we say one causes the other?
steps: Look at the scatter plot. Guess how strong the link is.
See the real r.
Judge the headline, then look behind the data.
experiments.finding: A correlation can come from a hidden third variable, from cause running the other way, or from chance in a small sample. A real link can also be hidden when only part of the range is studied. Causal claims need a design that rules these out, usually random assignment.
theory: Pearson's r runs from -1 to +1. Near 0 means no straight-line link; near ±1 means the points lie close to a line. r says nothing on its own about why.

Third variable: something else (age, temperature, illness severity) drives both. Reverse causation: Y causes X, not the other way. Chance: small samples swing wildly, so a striking r in a few people is easy to get by luck, and easier still if only the striking studies are reported.
Restricted range: if you only look at people who are all high on X (for example, only students already admitted), the link can shrink towards zero even when it is real across everyone.
When people are randomly assigned to different levels of X, third variables and reverse causation are ruled out, so a link can be read as cause.
The data here are generated by the computer with a known structure. They are not real studies.
clinic: Many findings in mental health are correlations: screen time and low mood, cannabis and psychosis, poverty and depression. Each needs the question: what else could explain this, and which way does it run?
Patients who attend more sessions are often more unwell, not made worse by sessions. Reading clinic data without thinking about severity leads to wrong conclusions.
Small pilot studies with impressive correlations often shrink when repeated with more people. Treat them as ideas to test, not facts.

evidence.note: These are basic statistical facts. How large a sample is needed for a stable r depends on the true size of the link; a few hundred is a common rough guide.

refs: Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for generalized causal inference. Houghton Mifflin.
Schönbrodt, F. D., & Perugini, M. (2013). At what sample size do correlations stabilize? Journal of Research in Personality, 47(5), 609 to 612.
Simmons, J. P., Nelson, L. D., & Simonsohn, U. (2011). False-positive psychology. Psychological Science, 22(11), 1359 to 1366.

checks.q: Across towns, more hospitals go with more deaths. What is the best reading?
options: A third variable: bigger towns have more of both
checks.why: Population size drives both. Compare death rates per person instead.

checks.q: A study of 8 people finds r = 0.7 between chai and memory. What is the main worry?
options: With 8 people, a large r can easily appear by chance
checks.why: Small samples give unstable r values. Repeat with many more people before believing it.

checks.q: Which design best supports "X causes Y"?
options: A large survey with a strong r
Randomly assigning people to get X or not, then measuring Y
Asking people whether X helped them
Following one person for a year
checks.why: Random assignment rules out third variables and reverse causation.

experiments.reflect: Which trap fooled you most? Think of a mental health headline you have seen. Which trap could explain it?

experiments.title: Conservation tasks
experiments.hook: Same juice, taller glass. Read what children say, and work out how they are thinking.
experiments.question: How does children's reasoning about "the same amount" change as they grow?
steps: Watch each classic task: see the before and after.
Read what each child says.
Name their stage and the kind of reasoning.
experiments.finding: In Piaget's tasks, younger children often say the amount changed when only its shape or spread changed. Older children say it stayed the same, and explain why: it can be poured back, nothing was added, or one change balances another.
theory: Piaget called the stage from about 2 to 7 years pre-operational. Children's thinking is tied to how things look. They tend to focus on one feature at a time, such as the height of the juice. This is centration.

From about 7 to 11 years, in the concrete operational stage, children can hold two features in mind and reason about changes. Three classic reasons: reversibility (it can be undone), identity (nothing was added or taken away) and compensation (taller but thinner).
A child who gives the right answer but switches from one feature to another ("this one is taller... no, that one is wider") is still focusing on one feature at a time.

Later research found that children succeed earlier when the task makes more sense to them. For example, when a "naughty teddy" messes up the row by accident, more young children say the number is still the same. Asking the same question twice can also make a child think the answer should change. So the ages are rough, and depend on the task and on schooling and culture.
clinic: When explaining an illness or a medicine to a young child, use one idea at a time, concrete examples and things they can see or handle.

Children may change their answer when an adult asks the same question again, because they think the first answer was wrong. This matters in child interviews, including safeguarding interviews: avoid repeated and leading questions.
Stage ages are averages. A child who is "late" on a conservation task is not necessarily delayed; check language, schooling, anxiety with a stranger, and how the task was asked.

evidence.note: The basic pattern (younger children judge by appearance) is robust. Piaget's age norms and his strict stage boundaries are debated: simpler, more natural tasks show earlier competence, and timing varies across cultures and schooling.

refs: Piaget, J. (1952). The child's conception of number. Routledge & Kegan Paul.
McGarrigle, J., & Donaldson, M. (1974). Conservation accidents. Cognition, 3(4), 341 to 350.
Donaldson, M. (1978). Children's minds. Fontana.

checks.q: A 5-year-old says the flattened clay has more "because it's bigger now". Which idea fits?
checks.why: She is focusing on one feature (how wide it looks) and ignoring the others.

checks.q: "If you pour it back, it will be the same." Which kind of reasoning is this?
checks.why: The child mentally undoes the change.

checks.q: In the "naughty teddy" version, more young children conserve number. What does that suggest?
options: Children's ability depends partly on how the task is set up
checks.why: When the adult does not deliberately change the row, the question makes more sense, and children show more of what they know.

experiments.reflect: Think of a child you know. How would you explain a hospital visit or a blood test to them, using what you learned about how they reason?

experiments.title: Why did they do it?
experiments.hook: Was it the person or the situation? Decide, then learn what was really going on.
experiments.question: When we explain other people's behaviour, how much do we blame their character and miss their situation?
steps: Read what someone did.
Slide: how much was the person, how much the situation?
See the rest of the story, then rate again.
experiments.finding: Observers tend to explain others' behaviour by their character and underweight the situation, even when the situation is clearly strong. This is called the fundamental attribution error, or correspondence bias. How strong it is varies with culture.
theory: An attribution is the reason we give for a behaviour. A dispositional attribution points to the person (lazy, rude, careless). A situational attribution points to circumstances (no bus, bad news, a threat).

In a classic study, people read an essay that the writer had been told which side to argue. Readers still judged the writer's true opinion from the essay. The situation was known, and still underweighted.

The situation is often invisible to the observer, while the person is right in front of them. Judging character is also fast; correcting for the situation takes effort and is skipped when we are busy or tired.

The bias is not universal. A study comparing adults in India and the United States found that Indian adults used more situational and context explanations, and American adults more dispositional ones. The differences grew with age, suggesting they are learned.
clinic: Labels like "non-compliant", "attention-seeking" or "unmotivated" in case notes are attributions. They can hide a situation: cost, travel, side effects, fear, or not understanding the plan.
A good formulation asks about situations as well as traits: what led up to it, what keeps it going, and what protects the person. That is where change is often possible.
Stigma often works through attribution: seeing mental illness or addiction as weakness of character makes blame and rejection more likely. Explaining the situation and the illness can reduce blame.

evidence.note: Correspondence bias is well replicated in Western samples. Its size depends on culture, task and motivation, and a related idea (that people explain their own behaviour by situation but others' by character) is weaker than once thought.

refs: Jones, E. E., & Harris, V. A. (1967). The attribution of attitudes. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 3(1), 1 to 24.

Ross, L. (1977). The intuitive psychologist and his shortcomings: Distortions in the attribution process. In L. Berkowitz (Ed.), Advances in experimental social psychology (Vol. 10, pp. 173 to 220). Academic Press.
Miller, J. G. (1984). Culture and the development of everyday social explanation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 46(5), 961 to 978.
Gilbert, D. T., & Malone, P. S. (1995). The correspondence bias. Psychological Bulletin, 117(1), 21 to 38.
Malle, B. F. (2006). The actor-observer asymmetry in attribution: A (surprising) meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(6), 895 to 919.

checks.q: The case notes say a patient is "non-compliant" after missing three appointments. What is the first useful step?
options: Ask what got in the way (cost, travel, side effects, understanding)
checks.why: "Non-compliant" is an attribution to the person. Finding the situational barrier is often what fixes it.

checks.q: In the essay study, readers knew the writer was told which side to argue. What did they still do?
options: Judged the writer's real opinion from the essay
checks.why: Even a known, strong situation was underweighted. That is correspondence bias.

checks.q: What did cross-cultural work comparing India and the United States suggest?
options: The bias is the same everywhere
Explanation styles differ by culture and are partly learned
checks.why: Indian adults gave more context-based explanations, and the gap grew with age.

experiments.reflect: Think of the last time someone annoyed you. What situation might they have been in that you could not see?

BIAS_CASES.text: The referral letter says "known case of anxiety". The 45-year-old describes chest tightness and breathlessness on climbing stairs. The trainee writes "panic symptoms" and moves on.
BIAS_CASES.why: The first label in the letter set the frame. Exertional chest symptoms in a 45-year-old need a medical check first.
fixes: Ask what else could explain it and check physical causes first
Increase the anxiety medicine
Reassure and discharge

BIAS_CASES.text: Last week the team saw a rare case of autoimmune encephalitis. This week, every young person with new psychosis is being sent for a lumbar puncture.
BIAS_CASES.why: A vivid recent case makes the rare diagnosis feel common. Base rates have not changed.
fixes: Order the test for everyone to be safe
Use base rates and specific red flags to decide who needs it
Ignore the rare diagnosis

BIAS_CASES.text: A trainee is sure a student has ADHD. In the interview they ask only about distraction and restlessness, and do not ask about sleep, mood or substance use.
BIAS_CASES.why: Only questions that could confirm the idea were asked. Poor sleep, low mood and substances all cause poor focus.
fixes: Ask questions that could prove the idea wrong
Give a rating scale to confirm
Ask the same questions twice

BIAS_CASES.text: Within ten minutes a patient is diagnosed with depression. Later, routine blood tests show a very underactive thyroid, but nobody looks at them because the diagnosis is already made.
BIAS_CASES.why: Thinking stopped once a diagnosis felt complete. New information was not allowed to change it.
fixes: Keep a working differential and review results before finalising
Make diagnoses faster
Avoid ordering blood tests

BIAS_CASES.text: A young woman with an intellectual disability becomes withdrawn and stops eating. Staff say "that is her behaviour". She has an untreated dental abscess.
BIAS_CASES.why: A change in behaviour was put down to the known disability. Pain is a common cause of behaviour change in people who cannot easily describe it.
fixes: Treat any change in behaviour as possibly physical and examine
Increase supervision
Wait and see

BIAS_CASES.text: A quiet, tidy, articulate man with a good job is felt to be "low risk" after a suicide attempt, because he "does not look like" the patients who usually make attempts.
BIAS_CASES.why: Judging by how typical someone looks ignores actual risk factors such as the attempt itself.
fixes: Base the risk assessment on factors and history, not appearance
Trust the first impression
Ask him if he is at risk and accept the answer

BIAS_CASES.text: An older man is assumed to have dementia because he is confused. Nobody notices the confusion started two days ago and comes and goes. He has a urine infection.
BIAS_CASES.why: Age plus confusion triggered "dementia". A sudden, fluctuating onset points to delirium, which is urgent.
fixes: Ask when it started and whether it fluctuates
Start a dementia medicine
Book a memory clinic in three months

BIAS_CASES.text: After a news story about a celebrity with bipolar disorder, a trainee begins to see "hypomania" in every cheerful, talkative client.
BIAS_CASES.why: A memorable story inflates how often the condition seems to occur.
fixes: Check duration, change from usual self, and impairment before calling it
Refer every cheerful client
Avoid the diagnosis altogether

liquid.title: Liquid
liquid.before: Two identical glasses with the same amount of juice. The child agrees they are the same.
liquid.after: One glass is poured into a tall, thin glass while the child watches.
liquid.ask: Is there more juice in one glass, or the same?

number.title: Number
number.before: Two rows of six coins, lined up one to one. The child agrees they are the same.
number.after: One row is spread out so it is longer.
number.ask: Are there more coins in one row, or the same?

length.title: Length
length.before: Two sticks of the same length, lined up. The child agrees they are the same.
length.after: One stick is pushed along so it sticks out past the other.
length.ask: Is one stick longer, or are they the same?

mass.title: Clay
mass.before: Two equal balls of clay. The child agrees they are the same.
mass.after: One ball is rolled into a long sausage.
mass.ask: Is there more clay in one, or the same?

CONS_ITEMS.says: That one has more juice. It goes up higher.
CONS_ITEMS.why: She looks only at the height of the juice.

CONS_ITEMS.says: It's the same. If you pour it back into the first glass, it will come up to the same place.
This row has more. It goes all the way over here.
CONS_ITEMS.why: She judges by how long the row is, not how many coins.

CONS_ITEMS.says: Still six and six. You only moved them, you didn't put any more.
CONS_ITEMS.why: Nothing was added or taken away, so the number is the same. He is only 6, younger than Piaget's usual age: judge the reasoning, not the age.

CONS_ITEMS.says: This one is longer. See, it comes out here.
CONS_ITEMS.why: She looks at one end only.

CONS_ITEMS.says: Same. This one sticks out here, but the other one sticks out at the back.
CONS_ITEMS.why: He sees that the gain at one end is balanced at the other.

CONS_ITEMS.says: The sausage has more, it's long... no wait, the ball has more, it's fatter.
CONS_ITEMS.why: She switches features but still looks at one at a time, never both together.

CONS_ITEMS.says: The same. It got longer but it also got thinner.
CONS_ITEMS.why: She holds two features together: longer, but thinner.

ATTRIBUTION_CASES.act: A man at the hospital pharmacy counter starts shouting at the staff.
ATTRIBUTION_CASES.reveal: His young son is in the emergency ward. He has been sent between three counters for two hours to collect one injection.

ATTRIBUTION_CASES.act: A patient has missed two follow-up appointments. The notes say "non-compliant".
ATTRIBUTION_CASES.reveal: The clinic moved last month. The new one is two bus changes away, and each visit costs her a day's wages.

ATTRIBUTION_CASES.act: A student wrote a strong, one-sided essay in favour of a new exam rule.
ATTRIBUTION_CASES.reveal: The teacher told each student which side to argue. She was given the side "in favour".

ATTRIBUTION_CASES.act: A college student has not handed in three assignments and keeps missing class.
ATTRIBUTION_CASES.reveal: Her mother had a stroke last month. She is the main carer and also works evening shifts.

ATTRIBUTION_CASES.act: A young man on the ward refuses to leave his room, even for meals.
ATTRIBUTION_CASES.reveal: Another patient threatened him in the corridor last night. Staff did not see it.

ATTRIBUTION_CASES.act: At the child clinic, a mother gives one-word answers and seems uninterested.
ATTRIBUTION_CASES.reveal: She speaks Telugu. The forms and the doctor's questions were in Hindi and English, and she felt embarrassed to say she did not follow.

CORR_SCENARIOS.headline: Children with bigger feet read better, survey finds
CORR_SCENARIOS.why: Older children have bigger feet and read better. Age drives both.
CORR_SCENARIOS.behind: Filled dots are older children, hollow dots younger. Look within one age group at a time: the link is gone.

CORR_SCENARIOS.headline: More therapy sessions linked to worse depression
CORR_SCENARIOS.why: People who are more unwell are offered, and attend, more sessions. Severity drives attendance, not the other way.
CORR_SCENARIOS.behind: In this simulation, depression score was set first, and the number of sessions was made to follow it.

CORR_SCENARIOS.headline: Chai drinkers have sharper memory: study of 6 students
CORR_SCENARIOS.why: In the simulation there is no link at all. With 6 people, a striking r turns up by luck, especially if only the striking result is reported.
CORR_SCENARIOS.behind: This sample was picked as the most striking of many small samples drawn from a population with r = 0. Draw new samples to see how much r jumps.

CORR_SCENARIOS.headline: Entrance exam scores don't predict grades at top college
CORR_SCENARIOS.why: The college only admits the highest scorers, so everyone studied is bunched at the top. Across all applicants the link is clear.
CORR_SCENARIOS.behind: Grey dots are the applicants who were not admitted. Across everyone, the link is much stronger.

CORR_SCENARIOS.headline: Randomly assigned extra sleep improved next-day recall
CORR_SCENARIOS.why: Sleep was assigned at random, so third variables and reverse causation are ruled out. Still worth repeating, but the causal reading is fair.
CORR_SCENARIOS.behind: Because the amount of sleep was set by a coin toss, nothing about the students could have decided it.

CORR_SCENARIOS.headline: Days with more ice cream sold have more drownings
CORR_SCENARIOS.why: Hot days bring both more ice cream and more swimming.
CORR_SCENARIOS.behind: Filled dots are hot days, hollow dots cooler days. Look within one kind of day at a time: the link is gone.
